  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Simone Ricci
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_correspondence ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Corresponding author: <span id="id1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">simone.ricci@unifi.it</span>.</span></span></span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>DINFO (Department of Information Engineering), University of Florence, Italy
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>MICC (Media Integration and Communication Center)
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Niccolò Biondi
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Trento, Italy
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>DINFO (Department of Information Engineering), University of Florence, Italy
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>MICC (Media Integration and Communication Center)
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Contrastive vision-language models map visual and textual representations into a shared normalized embedding space, making cosine similarity the natural metric for cross-modal retrieval. A practical challenge arises during model upgrades: independently trained models generally produce incompatible representation spaces, so replacing a deployed model typically requires recomputing embeddings for the entire gallery, which is prohibitively expensive at scale.
Orthogonal post-hoc alignment can partially mitigate this problem by mapping new-model queries into the old-model gallery space. However, because independently trained models can differ in fine-grained representation structure, the orthogonal alignment remains approximate, leaving a residual angular discrepancy between the old-model query and the aligned new-model query.
We study whether interpolation along the spherical geodesic between these two normalized query representations can improve retrieval without re-indexing the gallery.
We characterize when this path contains an interior query direction closer to an idealized retrieval-optimal direction than either endpoint, and connect this characterization to Recall@<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> through a local margin-based certification result.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks and model families show that post-alignment spherical interpolation improves over orthogonal alignment alone, recovering backward-compatibility in most evaluated settings.
Consistent with our geometric characterization, per-query oracle analysis shows that retrieval-favorable interior points occur frequently in practice. Code is available at <a href="https://github.com/miccunifi/SLERP_backward_compatibility" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/miccunifi/SLERP_backward_compatibility</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) have become a standard foundation for multimodal retrieval and zero-shot classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>. By mapping images and text into a shared normalized embedding space, these models leverage cosine similarity for cross-modal retrieval and prompt-based classification.
As the ecosystem of pretrained models grows through public model releases and model hubs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, a practical question arises: how can a deployed retrieval system benefit from a stronger model without recomputing all embeddings produced by the old one?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This question is particularly important in large-scale retrieval systems. In many production deployments, galleries containing millions or billions of items have already been encoded and indexed, making index reconstruction after every model update computationally prohibitive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>.
Moreover, re-indexing may be infeasible when the original raw data are no longer accessible due to privacy constraints, storage limitations, or data retention policies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. In such settings, backward-compatible upgrades that preserve the existing index may be the only viable option.
Even when re-indexing is feasible, progressive upgrades create a migration period requiring compatibility with the existing gallery.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This compatibility challenge is increasingly common as advances in architectures, optimization, and training data drive frequent model upgrades <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
Yet such updates can compromise backward-compatibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> and alter the behavior of downstream applications in undesirable ways <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.
Independently trained models rarely produce directly comparable representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, so directly replacing a query encoder can break compatibility with an existing gallery. Backward-compatible training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> addresses this issue by imposing restrictive constraints on the new-model training that can degrade its performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.
A recent alternative is post-hoc alignment, which decouples model improvement from compatibility constraints by training the new model independently and restoring compatibility afterward through a lightweight mapping between representation spaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.
This approach is motivated by the manifold hypothesis and related views on latent-space convergence, which suggest that functionally similar models may differ largely by simple transformations of a shared latent structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For contrastive VLMs, orthogonal Procrustes provides a natural alignment map: embeddings are normalized and compared by cosine similarity, so the resulting orthogonal transformation preserves inner products and therefore the image–text geometry underlying retrieval and zero-shot classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.
Moreover, agreement of the multimodal similarity kernel between independently trained contrastive VLMs identifies a single orthogonal map shared across image and text encoders, enabling cross-modal transfer of an alignment estimated from one modality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.
Related unimodal literature further supports orthogonal transformations over unconstrained linear maps, particularly when the new model is more informative, as an isometry preserves rather than distorts its discriminative geometry <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.
However, independent training can induce representation differences that are not captured by a single global isometry.
Orthogonal post-hoc alignment is therefore approximate: the aligned new-model query embedding will not, in general, coincide with the embedding that the old model would have produced for the same input, especially when models share coarse semantic structure but differ in fine-grained organization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>.
Consistent with this observation, Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that a non-negligible residual angular mismatch remains after orthogonally aligning SigLIP2 to CLIP ViT-B/32, both on the alignment dataset and under zero-shot transfer.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Residual discrepancy after orthogonal alignment from SigLIP2 to CLIP ViT-B/32. We show two complementary views: the distribution of residual angular mismatch between paired embeddings from the two models, and a 2D t-SNE projection of the corresponding feature spaces.
The remaining angular mismatch after alignment suggests that the orthogonal map leaves a residual cross-model gap, motivating a post-alignment interpolation strategy.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the residual angular discrepancy, we treat the old-model query and the aligned new-model query as endpoints in a shared normalized representation space.
Rather than assuming that either endpoint is optimal for retrieval, we ask whether an intermediate direction along the spherical geodesic connecting them can be more effective against the old-model gallery.
Because retrieval is based on cosine similarity between normalized embeddings, the corresponding spherical interpolation is the minor geodesic between the two query directions. We parameterize this path using spherical linear interpolation (SLERP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, which traverses the geodesic at constant angular speed and therefore gives the interpolation weight a consistent geometric interpretation across queries.
We formalize this intuition by considering an idealized retrieval-optimal query direction, used only as an analytical reference, and characterizing when the interpolation geodesic contains an interior point with a smaller angular gap to this direction than either endpoint. Geometrically, this occurs exactly when the normalized projection of the retrieval-optimal direction onto the interpolation plane lies in the relative interior of the arc; otherwise, the optimum along the arc is attained at an endpoint. We then connect this angular characterization to top-<math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> retrieval through a margin perturbation bound and a local Recall@<math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> certification result.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We propose an approach that requires no model retraining or gradient-based optimization: the deployed gallery remains unchanged, while the new-model query is mapped into the old-model space by orthogonal Procrustes alignment and then interpolated with the old-model query using a fixed weight selected on the alignment support set.
Empirically, we evaluate backward-compatible cross-modal retrieval across multiple benchmarks and model families. Orthogonal alignment provides a useful shared coordinate system but often fails to achieve backward-compatibility on its own, whereas post-alignment spherical interpolation improves over orthogonal alignment and frequently restores compatibility.
Controlled ablations show that endpoint combination accounts for most of the mean retrieval improvement, while support-set weight selection primarily improves compatibility robustness. The weight selected on the same CC3M alignment support set used to estimate the Procrustes map transfers across retrieval datasets, achieving performance close to the per-dataset optimum without target-test tuning. A per-query oracle analysis, reported only as an upper bound, shows that retrieval-favorable interior positions occur frequently in practice; flip-rate analysis further reveals that the retrieval gains arise from a favorable balance between positive and negative retrieval flips. Finally, the approach remains effective when the gallery is re-indexed and in zero-shot classification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We geometrically characterize when spherical interpolation between old-model and aligned new-model queries contains an interior direction closer to an idealized retrieval-optimal direction than either endpoint, and connect this characterization to top-<math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> retrieval.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a query-side approach for contrastive VLM upgrades that combines orthogonal Procrustes alignment with spherical interpolation, requiring neither model retraining nor gradient-based optimization, using a fixed interpolation weight selected on the alignment support set, while leaving the deployed gallery unchanged.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We validate the approach across CLIP, SigLIP1, and SigLIP2 on Flickr30k, COCO2014, and NoCaps, showing gains over orthogonal alignment and frequent backward-compatibility recovery. Ablations show that endpoint combination drives most of the improvement, while support-set weight selection transfers across datasets without target-test tuning.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Backward-compatible representation learning.</span>
Backward-compatible training (BCT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> formalized how to upgrade a retrieval model without re-encoding a deployed gallery by requiring embeddings from the new model to remain directly comparable with those of the old one. Subsequent work extended this paradigm through class- and prototype-level alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, neighborhood-level compatibility constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, open-set and universal formulations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, regression-aware hot-refresh updates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>, basis expansion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, stationary representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, and orthogonal transformation layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.
In particular, stationary representations learned with <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-Simplex fixed classifiers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, the geometry that also emerges under neural collapse <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, provably satisfy the inequality constraints of the formal compatibility definition in unimodal retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.
Other works relax the uniform compatibility requirement through selective compatibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, hyperbolic embeddings constrained by entailment cones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>, or perturbed prototype targets that preserve discriminative structure while maintaining interoperability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>. Recent work also shows that hyperspherical simplex representations derived for classifier outputs can be inherently backward-compatible and satisfy the formal definition of backward compatibility on average <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>. Related lifelong formulations have been studied in image-to-image retrieval and person re-identification, where compatibility avoids re-indexing across sequential updates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.
However, most of this literature addresses unimodal model upgrades. For vision-language models, XBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite> extends backward-compatible learning to cross-modal retrieval by learning a projection module, pretraining it on text, injecting Gaussian noise, and fine-tuning the new VLM with LoRA using both text and image data. While effective, this requires a dedicated training pipeline with large text and image–text corpora. In contrast, our approach requires no model retraining or gradient-based optimization: it estimates an orthogonal Procrustes map from a small alignment support set and performs query-side interpolation without modifying either model or re-indexing the gallery.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model interpolation.</span>
Interpolation has been studied extensively in parameter space through mode connectivity, weight averaging, model soups, permutation-aware merging, and task arithmetic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>.
Recent works also use spherical interpolation, but for different objects and objectives.
In zero-shot composed image retrieval, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite> uses SLERP to combine image and text embeddings into a composed query, together with text-anchored tuning. WARP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>, by contrast, applies SLERP in policy weight space to merge independently fine-tuned language-model policies, improving reward while controlling deviation from a reference policy.
Unlike these works, we apply spherical interpolation on the query side for backward-compatible retrieval, interpolating between the old-model query and the Procrustes-aligned new-model query for the same input. We characterize when the resulting minor geodesic contains an interior direction closer to an idealized retrieval-optimal direction than either endpoint, and connect this geometry to Recall@<math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> through margin-based guarantees.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We provide an extended discussion of post-hoc alignment, cross-model correspondence, and the geometry of contrastive vision-language representations in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Additional Related Work ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a deployed cross-modal retrieval system whose gallery is fixed and encoded by an old contrastive VLM
<math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{\mathrm{old}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{S}^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>old</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{\mathrm{old}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{S}^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where
<math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|z\|=1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|z\|=1\}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the input space, which may contain either images or text.
Suppose that an independently trained new model
<math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{\mathrm{new}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{S}^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{\mathrm{new}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{S}^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math>
becomes available.
Our goal is to use the new model on the query side while keeping the gallery indexed by the old model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math> be an alignment support set, disjoint from the gallery set
<math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}=\{g_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{g}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}=\{g_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{g}}</annotation></semantics></math>
and the query set
<math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}=\{x_{k}\}_{k=1}^{N_{q}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}=\{x_{k}\}_{k=1}^{N_{q}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For each <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}\in\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}\in\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, define
<math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}:=\phi_{\mathrm{old}}(x_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>old</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}:=\phi_{\mathrm{old}}(x_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{v}_{i}:=\phi_{\mathrm{new}}(x_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{v}_{i}:=\phi_{\mathrm{new}}(x_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>,
and stack these embeddings row-wise into
<math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U,\bar{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>V</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U,\bar{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We estimate the new-to-old alignment map by solving the orthogonal Procrustes problem:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\star}=\arg\min_{R^{\top}R=I}\|\bar{V}R-U\|_{F}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>V</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\star}=\arg\min_{R^{\top}R=I}\|\bar{V}R-U\|_{F}^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">If
<math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{V}^{\top}U=P\Sigma Q^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>V</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{V}^{\top}U=P\Sigma Q^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>
is its singular value decomposition, the closed-form solution is
<math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\star}=PQ^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\star}=PQ^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Since <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is orthogonal, the aligned representation preserves the inner-product geometry of the new model while expressing it in the old-model coordinate system.
For clarity, we develop the main analysis in the equal-dimensional case
<math id="S3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{\mathrm{old}},\phi_{\mathrm{new}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>old</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{\mathrm{old}},\phi_{\mathrm{new}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>;
the extension to unequal-dimensional model pairs using rectangular Procrustes is described in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Extension to Unequal Embedding Dimensions via Rectangular Procrustes ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For any query <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, define</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u(x):=\phi_{\mathrm{old}}(x)\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\qquad v(x):=\phi_{\mathrm{new}}(x)R^{\star}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>old</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u(x):=\phi_{\mathrm{old}}(x)\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\qquad v(x):=\phi_{\mathrm{new}}(x)R^{\star}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">as the old-model query and the aligned new-model query, respectively.
Thus, <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v(x)</annotation></semantics></math> are two normalized representations of the same input, both directly comparable with the old-model gallery.
Because the alignment is approximate for independently trained models, these query directions generally remain distinct, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We now characterize when interpolation between <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v(x)</annotation></semantics></math> can yield a direction closer to a retrieval-favorable direction than either endpoint.
For normalized embeddings <math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a,b\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a,b\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, define the spherical angle
<math id="S3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\angle(a,b):=\arccos\bigl(\langle a,b\rangle\bigr)\in[0,\pi]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\angle(a,b):=\arccos\bigl(\langle a,b\rangle\bigr)\in[0,\pi]</annotation></semantics></math>.
For a fixed query <math id="S3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, let
<math id="S3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta:=\angle(u(x),v(x))\in(0,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta:=\angle(u(x),v(x))\in(0,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math>.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          The condition <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0&lt;\theta&lt;\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0&lt;\theta&lt;\pi</annotation></semantics></math> excludes the coincident case <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u(x)=v(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u(x)=v(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and the antipodal case <math id="footnote1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos(\theta)=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos(\theta)=-1</annotation></semantics></math>, for which the minor geodesic is not uniquely defined.</span></span></span>
Since the analysis is pointwise, we omit the dependence on <math id="S3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and write <math id="S3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.
The problem then reduces to interpolation between two unit vectors along their minor geodesic.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmdefinition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmdefinition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmdefinition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(SLERP)<span id="Thmdefinition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmdefinition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u,v\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u,v\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math>, the SLERP query at interpolation weight <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> is</span></p>

</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">SLERP traces the unique minor geodesic from <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> at constant angular speed:</p>

</table>
<p id="S3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">Thus, <math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> has a direct geometric interpretation as the normalized angular displacement from the old-model query toward the aligned new-model query.
NLERP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> traces the same minor geodesic up to a monotone reparameterization and therefore attains the same optimal directions under continuous weight selection.
We use SLERP because its constant-angular-speed parameterization gives the interpolation weight a consistent geometric meaning across queries; Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Relationship Between SLERP and NLERP ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> discusses both interpolations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To formalize whether interpolation moves toward a retrieval-favorable direction, let

denote an idealized retrieval-optimal query direction, used only as an analytical reference.
For an interpolated query <math id="S3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math>, define the angular retrieval gap</p>

<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">

<math id="S3.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{span}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>span</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{span}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math>.

<p id="S3.p7.2" class="ltx_p">so that</p>

<div id="Thmlemma1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmlemma1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 1</span></span><span id="Thmlemma1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Decomposition relative to the interpolation plane; proof in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Decomposition of the Retrieval-Optimal Direction ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>)<span id="Thmlemma1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmlemma1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmlemma1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmlemma1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
There exist unique vectors
<math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\operatorname{span}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>span</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\operatorname{span}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\perp}\perp\operatorname{span}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo>⟂</mo><mrow><mi>span</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\perp}\perp\operatorname{span}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> such that
<math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}=p+w_{\perp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}=p+w_{\perp}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho:=\|p\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho:=\|p\|</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|w_{\perp}\|^{2}=1-\rho^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|w_{\perp}\|^{2}=1-\rho^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a unique
<math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\psi\in(-\pi,\pi]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi\in(-\pi,\pi]</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>

</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S3.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> measures the magnitude of the component of <math id="S3.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> in the interpolation plane, while <math id="S3.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> gives its angular coordinate from <math id="S3.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>.
The effect of interpolation is therefore determined by the position of the normalized in-plane projection relative to the arc <math id="S3.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,\theta]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,\theta]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>

<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Angular retrieval gap along the SLERP arc; proof in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Proof of Theorem ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>)<span id="Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\alpha}=\operatorname{slerp}(u,v;\alpha)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>slerp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\alpha}=\operatorname{slerp}(u,v;\alpha)</annotation></semantics></math> with
<math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math>,
and let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> be defined as in
Lemma <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1 (Decomposition relative to the interpolation plane; proof in Appendix ). ‣ 3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> with respect to
<math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{1}=u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{1}=u</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{2}=(v-\cos\theta\,u)/\sin\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{2}=(v-\cos\theta\,u)/\sin\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then:</span></p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(i)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">, then</span></p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="Thmtheorem1.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">holds if and only if the normalized in-plane projection of <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math>
lies strictly in the relative interior of the minor arc from <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Angular retrieval gap along the SLERP arc; proof in Appendix ). ‣ 3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that the endpoint separation <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> alone does not determine whether interpolation yields an interior angular improvement.
The decisive quantity is the position of the normalized in-plane projection of <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> relative to the minor arc.
If this direction lies in the relative interior of the arc, the geodesic contains an interior query closer to <math id="S3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> than either endpoint; otherwise, the optimum along the arc is attained at an endpoint.
Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Connection Between SLERP and Recall@𝐾 ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> connects this angular characterization to Recall@<math id="S3.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> by instantiating <math id="S3.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> as a top-<math id="S3.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-margin-optimal direction.
A margin perturbation bound then specifies when angular proximity to this direction locally certifies Recall@<math id="S3.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> success.
Thus, Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Angular retrieval gap along the SLERP arc; proof in Appendix ). ‣ 3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> characterizes when interpolation improves the angular retrieval gap, while the margin result determines when this improvement is sufficient for the discrete top-<math id="S3.p9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> retrieval event.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate whether post-alignment spherical interpolation improves backward-compatible retrieval after mapping the new model into the old-model coordinate system with orthogonal Procrustes alignment.
Because the alignment is obtained in closed form from a singular value decomposition (Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), we refer to it as SVD throughout this paper.
The main experiments focus on cross-modal retrieval with a fixed old-model gallery, while Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Cross-Modal Zero-shot Classification ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> reports an auxiliary zero-shot classification evaluation with fixed old-model text prototypes.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the proposed approach across CLIP, SigLIP1, and SigLIP2 vision-language models.
To cover both same-family and cross-family upgrades, we use OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, CLIP ViT-H/14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite>, SigLIP1 ViT-SO400M-14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and SigLIP2 ViT-SO400M-14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.
These produce embeddings of 512 (CLIP ViT-B/32), 768 (CLIP ViT-L/14), 1024 (CLIP ViT-H/14), and 1152 (SigLIP1/2) dimensions, covering equal- and unequal-dimensional model pairs.
Including SigLIP-family models allows us to assess whether the residual post-alignment discrepancy and the gains from spherical interpolation extend beyond CLIP-family representation geometry to models trained with different objectives.
All checkpoints are obtained from the OpenCLIP repository <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each old–new model pair, we estimate the Procrustes map from
12,637 available image–text pairs from the CC3M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>
validation split, which serves as the alignment support set.
We consider three support-modality choices: text-only, image-only, and joint image–text support, where the joint setting stacks embeddings from both modalities before solving the Procrustes problem.
Motivated by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, these variants test whether a single modality is sufficient to estimate the orthogonal map and whether combining modalities yields more stable cross-modal transfer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate backward-compatible retrieval, comparing the training-based XBT baseline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, three Procrustes support-modality variants, and SLERP applied after each alignment.
Old- and new-model performance are included as reference points.
For SLERP, <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the old-model query, while <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the SVD-aligned new-model query, i.e., the SVD baseline.
For each old–new model pair, the Procrustes map is estimated and the interpolation weight <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected on the same CC3M alignment support set.
Separate weights are selected for image-to-text (I2T) and text-to-image (T2I) retrieval by maximizing CC3M Recall@1 over
<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,1.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,1.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
These model-pair- and retrieval-direction-specific weights are then fixed for
evaluation on three cross-modal retrieval benchmarks, following the large-scale
protocol of XBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>: the full Flickr30k dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite> (the union of the Karpathy splits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>), and the validation splits of COCO 2014 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite> and NoCaps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite>.
We additionally report the benchmark-specific oracle weight <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, selected directly on each test benchmark solely as an upper-bound reference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Cross-modal backward-compatible retrieval for same-family model upgrades.
For each dataset, the <math id="S4.T1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> column reports the interpolation weights for
I2T/T2I retrieval.
The Sup. column indicates the support modality used to estimate the Procrustes map: text-only (T), image-only (I), or joint image–text (I+T).
The weight <math id="S4.T1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected on CC3M and fixed
across all test datasets, whereas <math id="S4.T1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected directly on each
test dataset and is reported only as an oracle upper bound.
Checkmarks indicate backward compatibility; bold and underlined values denote
the best and second-best <math id="S4.T1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{new}\!\to\!\mathrm{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>new</mi><mo lspace="0.128em" rspace="0.128em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{new}\!\to\!\mathrm{old}</annotation></semantics></math> results, respectively.
</span></figcaption>
