<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Evaluation Protocol</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>,
we consider an updated system empirically backward-compatible if, given a
performance metric <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, the new-to-old performance strictly exceeds the
old-to-old performance, i.e.,</p>
<table id="S4.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}&gt;M_{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>new</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>old</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}&gt;M_{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>old</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math> evaluates old-model queries against
the fixed old-model gallery, whereas <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>new</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>
evaluates the updated query representations against the same old-model gallery.
We use Recall@<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\{1,5,10\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\{1,5,10\}</annotation></semantics></math>, as the retrieval metric <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>
and report results for both image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, we further analyze
positive and negative retrieval flips relative to the old-to-old system.
For each query <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, let
<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{i}^{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>old</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i}^{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{i}^{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>new</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i}^{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>
indicate whether retrieval is successful under the corresponding system,
where success means that at least one relevant gallery item appears among
the top-<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> retrieved items.
The positive-flip rate (<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{PFR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>PFR</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{PFR}</annotation></semantics></math>) and negative-flip rate
(<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{NFR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>NFR</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{NFR}</annotation></semantics></math>) are defined as</p>
<table id="S4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E16"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{PFR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>PFR</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{PFR}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[c_{i}^{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}=0,\;c_{i}^{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}=1\right]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>old</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>new</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[c_{i}^{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}=0,\;c_{i}^{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}=1\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S4.E17"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{NFR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>NFR</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{NFR}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E17.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[c_{i}^{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}=1,\;c_{i}^{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}=0\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>old</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>new</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>old</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[c_{i}^{\mathrm{old}\to\mathrm{old}}=1,\;c_{i}^{\mathrm{new}\to\mathrm{old}}=0\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Thus, positive flips correspond to queries that become successful after
the upgrade, whereas negative flips correspond to queries that become unsuccessful.
Since Recall@<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> is the average of these binary success indicators, its change relative to the old-to-old system satisfies:</p>
<table id="S4.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathrm{R@}K=\mathrm{PFR}-\mathrm{NFR}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>PFR</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>NFR</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathrm{R@}K=\mathrm{PFR}-\mathrm{NFR}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Cross-modal backward-compatible retrieval for cross-family model upgrades.
For each dataset, the <math id="S4.T2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> column reports the interpolation weights for
I2T/T2I retrieval.
The Sup. column indicates the support modality used to estimate the Procrustes map: text-only (T), image-only (I), or joint image–text (I+T).
The weight <math id="S4.T2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected on CC3M and fixed
across all test datasets, whereas <math id="S4.T2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected directly on each
test dataset and is reported only as an oracle upper bound.
Checkmarks indicate backward compatibility; bold and underlined values denote

<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Compatibility Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tables <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> report cross-modal compatible retrieval results for same-family and cross-family model pairs, respectively.
Across 90 evaluations—five model pairs, three support modalities, three datasets, and both retrieval directions—CC3M-selected SLERP satisfies the Recall@1 compatibility criterion in Eq. <a href="#S4.E15" title="In 4.2 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> in 85 cases, compared with 45 for SVD alone.
The additional model-pair results included in this aggregate, together with the full Recall@1/5/10 results, are reported in Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Detailed Retrieval Performance ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>.
SVD thus provides an effective post-hoc alignment but does not consistently satisfy the compatibility criterion, particularly for cross-family pairs.
This is consistent with the residual angular discrepancy in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>: Procrustes alignment maps new representations into the old-model coordinate system but does not fully resolve the cross-model mismatch.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For same-family upgrades, our approach remains competitive with available XBT results without any specific compatibility training.
In the harder SigLIP1 <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> CLIP ViT-H/14 setting, where the new model is not uniformly stronger than the old one, SLERP still achieves compatibility in most cases.
These results suggest that the gains arise from combining old and SVD-aligned new representations, rather than solely from a stronger new encoder. Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Compatibility Results ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates this behavior for T2I Recall@1, with performance often maximized at an interior interpolation weight.
The CC3M-selected <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> closely tracks the dataset-specific oracle <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, showing that a single support-set-selected weight transfers to Flickr30k, COCO, and NoCaps without test-set tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Additional SLERP Arc Results ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> reports the corresponding I2T curves, which show the same pattern.
Across different support set modalities, text-only alignment is the most stable choice overall.
Image-only support, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, and joint support remain competitive in individual cases, but text embeddings appear to provide cleaner semantic anchors for estimating the old–new alignment.
Moreover, Appendix <a href="#A13" title="Appendix M Per-Query Oracle Analysis ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">M</span></a> provides a complementary per-query oracle analysis on Flickr30k I2T retrieval for CLIP ViT-L/14 <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> CLIP ViT-B/32.
Among queries achieving Recall@1 at some evaluated interpolation weight, <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="97.65\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>97.65</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">97.65\%</annotation></semantics></math> are assigned an interior oracle weight. The oracle uses query-level test labels and is therefore non-deployable, it provides observable evidence consistent with the geometric characterization in Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>: retrieval-favorable query representations frequently occur in the interior of the interpolation arc rather than at either endpoint.
Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Re-indexing ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a> further shows that SLERP often improves over the new model even when re-indexing is allowed, indicating that the benefit of interpolation is not limited to the compatibility-only setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, in Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Target-Set Budget Sensitivity ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a> we evaluate the setting in which a small subset from the target test distribution is available for estimating the SLERP weight. The results show that even a modest subset is sufficient to select a reliable dataset-specific interpolation weight.
We further show in Appendix <a href="#A14" title="Appendix N Alignment and Endpoint-Combination Baselines ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">N</span></a> that the gains are not specific to SLERP: a fixed normalized midpoint, support-set selected NLERP, and score interpolation yield comparable average improvements. We use SLERP for its constant-angular-speed parameterization, which gives the interpolation weight a consistent geometric interpretation across queries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flip analysis.</span>
Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Compatibility Results ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> decomposes the T2I Recall@1 change along the interpolation path into positive and negative flips relative to old-to-old retrieval.
Since <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathrm{R@1}=\mathrm{PFR}-\mathrm{NFR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>PFR</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>NFR</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathrm{R@1}=\mathrm{PFR}-\mathrm{NFR}</annotation></semantics></math>, the optimal interpolation weight is determined by the balance between the two rates rather than by positive flips alone.
Moving from the old-model query toward the aligned new-model query initially corrects more old-model failures than it introduces regressions; beyond the optimum, negative flips grow faster than positive ones and the gain decreases.
For CLIP ViT-H/14 <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> CLIP ViT-B/32, where SVD alignment alone already exceeds the old model, the gain peaks close to the SVD endpoint (<math id="S4.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\star}=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{\star}=0.7</annotation></semantics></math>). For SigLIP1 <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> CLIP ViT-H/14, where the SVD-aligned query induces a high negative-flip rate, the gain peaks close to the old-model endpoint (<math id="S4.SS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\star}=0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{\star}=0.2</annotation></semantics></math>), and interpolation retains most old-model successes while still recovering part of the new-model gains.
In both cases, the CC3M-selected <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> lies near the peak.
Appendix <a href="#A12" title="Appendix L Additional Flip Analyses ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">L</span></a> extends the analysis to I2T retrieval and NoCaps dataset.</p>
</div>

The blue curve reports <math id="S4.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathrm{R@1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathrm{R@1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Here <math id="S4.F4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to old-model queries and <math id="S4.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> to SVD-aligned new-model queries.
Red and blue markers denote the dataset-specific oracle <math id="S4.F4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> and the CC3M-selected weight <math id="S4.F4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We studied the problem of upgrading contrastive vision-language retrieval systems without re-encoding the deployed gallery.
Motivated by the residual angular discrepancy left by orthogonal post-hoc alignment, we proposed a query-side approach that first maps new-model queries into the old-model representation space through orthogonal Procrustes alignment and then interpolates them with the corresponding old-model queries along the spherical geodesic.
Our analysis characterizes when this interpolation path contains an interior direction closer to an idealized retrieval-optimal direction than either endpoint, and connects this angular improvement to Recall@<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> through a local margin-based sufficient condition.
Empirically, we validated the method across CLIP, SigLIP1, and SigLIP2 upgrades, covering same-family and cross-family pairs and Flickr30k, COCO, and NoCaps retrieval benchmarks.
SLERP improves over SVD alignment in nearly all settings, often restores empirical backward-compatibility, and frequently matches or surpasses training-based compatibility baselines while requiring no compatibility training.
The support-set selected interpolation weights transfer reliably across datasets, and additional evaluations show that the same mechanism also extends to re-indexed retrieval and zero-shot classification.
Overall, these results show that residual post-alignment geometry contains useful retrieval signal and that post-alignment interpolation provides a simple and effective mechanism for backward-compatible vision-language model upgrades.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations.</span>
SLERP also involves practical trade-offs, discussed in Appendix <a href="#A15" title="Appendix O Limitations ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">O</span></a>: the interpolation weight must be selected on a support set, query-side inference requires both endpoint embeddings, and performance remains bounded by the quality and complementarity of the available representations.
In our experiments, these trade-offs are favorable, suggesting that spherical interpolation provides a simple, robust approach for upgrading contrastive vision-language retrieval systems while preserving backward-compatibility. Moreover, it provides a compatibility mechanism during model migration, allowing the deployed gallery to remain usable while full re-indexing is deferred or performed offline, as described in Appendix <a href="#A16" title="Appendix P Deployment Cost and Migration-Period Analysis ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">P</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Appendix Contents</h2>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Additional Related Work</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Post-hoc alignment and cross-model correspondence.</span>
A complementary line of work studies whether the latent spaces of independently trained models can be aligned after training, without modifying the original model weights. Classical manifold alignment and Procrustes methods provide the foundation for this approach by seeking simple correspondences between representation spaces, either from paired anchors or by preserving the geometric structure of the underlying data manifolds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>, <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite>. The central assumption is that independently trained models may encode similar semantic structure in different coordinate systems; consequently, a lightweight post-hoc transformation can often make their representations comparable. Recent work supports this view in latent representation spaces, showing that useful cross-model correspondences can be recovered through semantic latent translation and latent functional maps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>. These results suggest that exact equality between representation spaces is not required for interoperability—a transformation that preserves the task-relevant structure shared across models can be sufficient.
This perspective is consistent with broader evidence that independently trained models can develop similar representation geometry across architectures and modalities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>. However, such convergence is generally approximate rather than exact, and recent results indicate that cross-modal agreement may weaken at realistic scales and in many-to-many settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. Most closely related to our setting, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> shows that independently trained contrastive VLMs can often be approximately canonicalized by a single orthogonal map shared across modalities, estimated from a small anchor set and without retraining either model. Recent work further extends this viewpoint beyond pairwise alignment by constructing a shared orthogonal reference space across multiple models and applying a retrieval-oriented correction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>]</cite>. These works support the assumption that a new-model query can be mapped into the coordinate system of the deployed gallery model with post-hoc orthogonal alignment. Our work focuses on the angular discrepancy after this alignment step: even in a common coordinate system, embeddings of the same input may differ due to architecture, training data (e.g., label noise and long-tailed class distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>), optimization, or inductive bias, and may therefore induce different rankings over the same fixed gallery. We study this residual discrepancy directly by characterizing when spherical interpolation between the old-model query and the aligned new-model query improves retrieval.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A related line of work combines independently trained embedding models directly in parameter space. In particular, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite> studies model merging for general text embeddings by searching over combinations of task vectors, including SLERP-based interpolation; unlike our setting, this operates in model-parameter space and assumes models with the same architecture, whereas we interpolate query representations after cross-model alignment.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Geometry of contrastive vision-language spaces.</span>
Our analysis builds on work showing that contrastive VLMs learn a normalized image–text embedding space in which cross-modal comparisons are performed by cosine similarity, but whose geometry is not fully homogeneous or modality-invariant <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite>.
Prior work shows that image and text embeddings can occupy separated regions of the representation space, leading to modality gaps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>, <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>. Other studies identify intra-modal misalignment within individual encoders <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>]</cite>, as well as spectral decompositions into approximately isotropic shared components and anisotropic modality-specific directions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">81</a>]</cite>. Recent work further suggests that InfoNCE-trained representations may exhibit approximately Gaussian embedding distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>]</cite>.
Together, these findings indicate that global comparability does not imply full geometric equivalence: a common coordinate system may preserve cross-modal similarity while still retaining model-specific or modality-specific structure. This perspective helps explain why an alignment estimated from one modality can transfer to the other <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, while also leaving residual angular discrepancies after alignment. In our setting, this residual angular structure is precisely the object of interest, and it motivates interpolation between the old-model query and the aligned new-model query.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Extension to Unequal Embedding Dimensions via Rectangular Procrustes</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We describe how the alignment obtained by solving the Procrustes problem used in the main text extends when the old model and the new model have different embedding dimensions. Let the old model, which defines the deployed gallery space, produce normalized embeddings in <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{old}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{old}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and let the new model produce normalized embeddings in <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Given an alignment support set, denote by</p>

<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">First consider the case <math id="A2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{new}}&lt;d_{\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{new}}&lt;d_{\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Since the new-model representation has lower dimension than the old-model representation, it can be embedded isometrically into the old-model gallery space. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E27.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\star}=PQ^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}\times d_{\mathrm{old}}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\star}=PQ^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}\times d_{\mathrm{old}}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(27)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p4.4" class="ltx_p">Because</p>
<table id="A2.E28" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E28.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\star}R^{\star\top}=PQ^{\top}QP^{\top}=I_{d_{\mathrm{new}}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>⋆</mo><mo lspace="0em">⁣</mo><mo>⊤</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\star}R^{\star\top}=PQ^{\top}QP^{\top}=I_{d_{\mathrm{new}}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(28)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p4.5" class="ltx_p">the map preserves all inner products within the new-model space. Indeed, for any <math id="A2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}}</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="A2.E29" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E29.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle xR^{\star},yR^{\star}\rangle=xR^{\star}R^{\star\top}y^{\top}=xy^{\top}=\langle x,y\rangle." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>⋆</mo><mo lspace="0em">⁣</mo><mo>⊤</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle xR^{\star},yR^{\star}\rangle=xR^{\star}R^{\star\top}y^{\top}=xy^{\top}=\langle x,y\rangle.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(29)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p4.6" class="ltx_p">Thus, when <math id="A2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{new}}&lt;d_{\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{new}}&lt;d_{\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the new aligned representation is an isometric embedding of the new-model representation into the old-model gallery space. Norms, angles, inner products, and cosine similarities between new-model embeddings are preserved exactly.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We now consider the case <math id="A2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{new}}&gt;d_{\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{new}}&gt;d_{\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>. In this setting, the new-model representation has higher dimension than the old-model gallery space, so no linear map from <math id="A2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{new}}}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{old}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{old}}}</annotation></semantics></math> can preserve all inner products. The rectangular Procrustes map should therefore be interpreted as a partial isometry: it extracts the <math id="A2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional component of the new-model representation that is maximally aligned with the old-model gallery space.</p>
</div>

</div>

<p id="A2.p7.3" class="ltx_p">This augmented representation preserves the full geometry of the new-model space. <tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(37)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p7.4" class="ltx_p">At the same time, the residual component is inert for retrieval against the deployed old-model gallery, since</p>
<table id="A2.E38" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="A2.p7.5" class="ltx_p">Thus, when <math id="A2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{new}}&gt;d_{\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{new}}&gt;d_{\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the projected vector <math id="A2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{v}R^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{v}R^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is the only component of the new aligned representation that affects cross-model retrieval in the old-model gallery space.
The residual block <math id="A2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{v}N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{v}N</annotation></semantics></math> preserves the remaining new-model geometry, but it has zero interaction with old-model gallery embeddings represented as <math id="A2.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,0)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, retrieval can be performed directly in the old-model gallery space using the projected new aligned embedding <math id="A2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{v}R^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{v}R^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="A2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{new}}&gt;d_{\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{new}}&gt;d_{\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>, this projection is not generally unit-norm:</p>
<table id="A2.E39" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E39.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\bar{v}R^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}=\bar{v}PP^{\top}\bar{v}^{\top}\leq\|\bar{v}\|_{2}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\bar{v}R^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}=\bar{v}PP^{\top}\bar{v}^{\top}\leq\|\bar{v}\|_{2}^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A2.p8.2" class="ltx_p">Multiplying all scores for a fixed query by a positive scalar does not change the induced ranking, so this norm reduction does not affect nearest-neighbor retrieval by itself. However, the SLERP analysis requires both endpoints to lie on the old-model unit sphere. We therefore normalize the projected new aligned query before interpolation:</p>

<p id="A2.p8.3" class="ltx_p">For <math id="A2.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{new}}\leq d_{\mathrm{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{new}}\leq d_{\mathrm{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the alignment is norm-preserving, so this normalization is redundant. <section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Relationship Between SLERP and NLERP</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix clarifies the relationship between spherical linear interpolation (SLERP) and normalized linear interpolation (NLERP) in our setting.
Both methods can interpolate between the same two normalized query endpoints: the old-model query embedding <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and the SVD-aligned new-model query embedding <math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="A3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The difference is not the set of directions that can be reached, but the way in which the interpolation path is parameterized.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recall that SLERP is defined as</p>
<table id="A3.E43" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E43.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\mathrm{slerp}}_{\alpha}=\frac{\sin((1-\alpha)\theta)}{\sin\theta}u+\frac{\sin(\alpha\theta)}{\sin\theta}v,\qquad\alpha\in[0,1]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>α</mi><mi>slerp</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\mathrm{slerp}}_{\alpha}=\frac{\sin((1-\alpha)\theta)}{\sin\theta}u+\frac{\sin(\alpha\theta)}{\sin\theta}v,\qquad\alpha\in[0,1].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(43)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">By contrast, NLERP first takes a Euclidean convex combination of the two endpoints and then renormalizes it:</p>
<table id="A3.E44" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E44.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\mathrm{nlerp}}_{\beta}=\frac{(1-\beta)u+\beta v}{\|(1-\beta)u+\beta v\|_{2}},\qquad\beta\in[0,1]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>β</mi><mi>nlerp</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\mathrm{nlerp}}_{\beta}=\frac{(1-\beta)u+\beta v}{\|(1-\beta)u+\beta v\|_{2}},\qquad\beta\in[0,1].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(44)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Thus, NLERP also remains on the unit sphere, but its interpolation weight does not correspond to constant angular motion along the arc.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To make the relationship explicit, use the same orthonormal basis as in Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>,</p>
<table id="A3.E45" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E45.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{1}=u,\qquad e_{2}=\frac{v-\cos\theta\,u}{\sin\theta}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{1}=u,\qquad e_{2}=\frac{v-\cos\theta\,u}{\sin\theta},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(45)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">so that <math id="A3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v=\cos\theta\,e_{1}+\sin\theta\,e_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v=\cos\theta\,e_{1}+\sin\theta\,e_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The unnormalized NLERP numerator can then be written as</p>
<table id="A3.E46" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E46.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1-\beta)u+\beta v=\bigl(1-\beta+\beta\cos\theta\bigr)e_{1}+\beta\sin\theta\,e_{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1-\beta)u+\beta v=\bigl(1-\beta+\beta\cos\theta\bigr)e_{1}+\beta\sin\theta\,e_{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(46)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Therefore, after normalization, the NLERP point has angular coordinate</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(47)</span></td></tr></tbody>

<p id="A3.p3.4" class="ltx_p">and</p>

</table>
<p id="A3.p3.5" class="ltx_p">Moreover,</p>
<table id="A3.E49" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E49.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{d\tau}{d\beta}=\frac{\sin\theta}{\|(1-\beta)u+\beta v\|_{2}^{2}}&gt;0," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mfrac><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d\tau}{d\beta}=\frac{\sin\theta}{\|(1-\beta)u+\beta v\|_{2}^{2}}&gt;0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(49)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.p3.6" class="ltx_p">so <math id="A3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(\beta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(\beta)</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly increasing on <math id="A3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.
Consequently, NLERP traces exactly the same minor geodesic arc as SLERP, but under a monotone reparameterization.
Conversely, the inverse mapping from a SLERP weight <math id="A3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> to the NLERP weight that reaches the same direction is</p>
<table id="A3.E50" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E50.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta(\alpha)=\frac{\sin(\alpha\theta)}{\sin((1-\alpha)\theta)+\sin(\alpha\theta)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta(\alpha)=\frac{\sin(\alpha\theta)}{\sin((1-\alpha)\theta)+\sin(\alpha\theta)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(50)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This equivalence has an immediate implication for continuous weight selection.
For any retrieval objective that depends only on the resulting query direction, optimizing over <math id="A3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> with SLERP and optimizing over <math id="A3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> with NLERP search over the same set of unit vectors.
Thus, in the continuous setting, the two methods have the same optimal directions.
The distinction is instead geometric and practical: SLERP moves at constant angular speed, since <math id="A3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\angle(u,q^{\mathrm{slerp}}_{\alpha})=\alpha\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>α</mi><mi>slerp</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\angle(u,q^{\mathrm{slerp}}_{\alpha})=\alpha\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas NLERP moves non-uniformly along the same arc.
Using SLERP therefore makes the interpolation weight directly interpretable as a normalized angular displacement from the old-model query toward the SVD-aligned new-model query.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Relationship Between SLERP and NLERP ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> empirically compares SLERP and NLERP on Flickr30k and COCO retrieval after SVD alignment.
The two curves are nearly identical across the interpolation path and achieve their best performance in the same interior region of the arc.
The small visible differences are consistent with the reparameterization above: a uniform grid in the NLERP weight <math id="A3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is not a uniform grid in angular position, and therefore does not sample exactly the same directions as a uniform grid in the SLERP weight <math id="A3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>.
Overall, this comparison supports our use of SLERP not because it accesses a different family of query representations, but because it provides a geometrically canonical parameterization of the same interpolation arc.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Decomposition of the Retrieval-Optimal Direction</h2>

<div id="Thmlemma2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmlemma2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma </span><a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1 (Decomposition relative to the interpolation plane; proof in Appendix ). ‣ 3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref ltx_font_bold"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a></span><span id="Thmlemma2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Decomposition relative to the interpolation plane)<span id="Thmlemma2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmlemma2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmlemma2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmlemma2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
There exist unique vectors
<math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\operatorname{span}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>span</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\operatorname{span}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\perp}\perp\operatorname{span}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo>⟂</mo><mrow><mi>span</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\perp}\perp\operatorname{span}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> such that
<math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}=p+w_{\perp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}=p+w_{\perp}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho:=\|p\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho:=\|p\|</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then <math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|w_{\perp}\|^{2}=1-\rho^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|w_{\perp}\|^{2}=1-\rho^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If <math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a unique
<math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\psi\in(-\pi,\pi]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi\in(-\pi,\pi]</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E51.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=\rho(\cos\psi\,e_{1}+\sin\psi\,e_{2})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ψ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ψ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=\rho(\cos\psi\,e_{1}+\sin\psi\,e_{2}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<div id="A4.2" class="ltx_proof">

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Proof of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Angular retrieval gap along the SLERP arc; proof in Appendix ). ‣ 3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a></h2>

<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem </span><a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Angular retrieval gap along the SLERP arc; proof in Appendix ). ‣ 3 Geometric Characterization of Spherical Interpolation for Compatible Retrieval ‣ Spherical Interpolation for Backward-Compatible Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref ltx_font_bold"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Angular retrieval gap along the SLERP arc)<span id="Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\alpha}=\operatorname{slerp}(u,v;\alpha)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>slerp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\alpha}=\operatorname{slerp}(u,v;\alpha)</annotation></semantics></math> with

holds if and only if the normalized in-plane projection of <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> lies strictly in the relative interior of the minor arc from <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>

<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Since <math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math>, the vectors <math id="A5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> are distinct and
non-antipodal, and hence span a two-dimensional interpolation plane. Define the
orthonormal basis</span></p>

<math id="A5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{span}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>span</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{span}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math>. Since every <math id="A5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> lies in this plane,</span></p>

<p id="A5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">We now prove (iii), again assuming <math id="A5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. Since <math id="A5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\arccos" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>arccos</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly
decreasing on <math id="A5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, minimizing <math id="A5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G(\alpha)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G(\alpha)</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to maximizing</span></p>

Moreover, since <math id="A5.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> lies strictly inside the interval and
<math id="A5.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta&lt;\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta&lt;\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, neither endpoint can attain the same value. <p id="A5.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">Combining the two directions, a strict interior improvement occurs if and only
if the normalized in-plane projection <math id="A5.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p/\|p\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p/\|p\|</annotation></semantics></math> lies strictly in the relative
interior of the minor arc from <math id="A5.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A5.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>.
∎</span></p>
